title: Adie’s Tonic Pupil: A Diagnostic Masterclass
summary: Tonic pupil represents a post-ganglionic parasympathetic denervation of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle. Precise localization is vital to differentiate benign Adie’s Tonic Pupil from sinister oculomotor nerve palsies or pharmacological blockade.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: Adie’s tonic pupil results from damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves. This leads to denervation supersensitivity of the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle to cholinergic agents. Pathologically, it involves a loss of ganglionic neurons, often associated with a viral or autoimmune etiology.

sections.title: Clinical Features
content: Slow, tonic near response (vermiform iris movement).
Reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes (Holmes-Adie Syndrome).

sections.title: Pharmacological Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Instill 0.125% Pilocarpine (dilute). Tonic pupil will constrict due to denervation supersensitivity.
Step 2: Normal pupil remains relatively unaffected by dilute pilocarpine.
Step 3: If pupil fails to constrict to 0.125%, consider 1% Pilocarpine to rule out pharmacological blockade (fixed pupil).
Step 4: Assess deep tendon reflexes to confirm Holmes-Adie syndrome.

rows: Bilateral, miotic, non-reactive to light, constricts to near

sections.title: Red Flags
content: Presence of ptosis or EOM restriction (Suggests CN III involvement).
Normal or hyperactive deep tendon reflexes (If suspected Adie's, seek other causes of autonomic dysfunction).

content.explanation: T: Tendon reflexes absent, O: Often unilateral, N: Near reaction slow, I: Iris vermiform movement, C: Cholinergic hypersensitivity (0.125% Pilocarpine).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always use a slit-lamp to check for sectorial iris palsy (vermiform movement).
Anisocoria in Adie's is often 'light-reversal' (less in dark, more in light).
Consider syphilis or diabetes in differential for secondary tonic pupils.
Management is typically observation; patient may need reading glasses for accommodative paresis.
